question: Do sit-stand desks reduce office workers' sitting time, and do they improve any measured health outcome?

coverage.note: We have the 2018 Cochrane pooled result: 100 min per workday at up to 3 months and 57 min at 3 to 12 months, from mixed measures. We have no pooled estimate from device-measured (activPAL or accelerometer) data only. We also have no meta-analysis published after 2018.

Cochrane shows the effect falling from 100 min to 57 min (only 2 studies) and has no data beyond 12 months. SMArT Work (desk plus programme) shows the effect growing to 83 min at 12 months. We have no device-measured data beyond 12 months, and no 12-month result from a second trial (for example Stand Up Victoria).

Cochrane 2018 (total sitting −82 min/day, 2 studies) and SMArT Work (total daily sitting −82 min/day at 12 months, device-measured) both show that workers did not make up the loss by sitting more outside work. The limit: this rests on few studies.

We know the SMART Work & Life design (programme plus desk, programme alone, control), but we have not found its results. Separately, one 8-week desk-only trial (self-reported) found −80 min. We have no direct comparison between the two intervention arms.

No outcome has yet been shown to be replicated. Cochrane 2016 found no effect on musculoskeletal symptoms, work performance or sick leave. SMArT Work improved only self-reported psychological and work outcomes. The cholesterol and HDL results each come from one small trial. We have no pooled GRADE-rated results for blood pressure, glucose, lipids, weight or pain from recent meta-analyses.

We only have the general Cochrane statement (small samples, low to very low quality). We have no assessment of statistical power or pre-registration for the trials that measured cardiometabolic outcomes (for example Stand Up Victoria biomarkers). We have no data on contamination between arms.

The UK Biobank standing study (standing not protective; more than 2 h/day linked to circulatory disease) is known only from the Sydney press release and the Guardian. We have not read the primary paper in the International Journal of Epidemiology. A small cross-sectional study found no link with varicose veins. We have no occupational-cohort evidence on standing and low-back or leg pain.

We have only a retail price (£360 to £375 for a desk-top add-on). We have not found the SMArT Work trial-based economic evaluation (cost per participant, cost-effectiveness from the employer and NHS viewpoints).

contradictions: Durability. The Cochrane pooled effect falls from 100 min/workday (up to 3 months) to 57 min (3 to 12 months, 2 studies), which suggests the novelty wears off. SMArT Work's device-measured effect grows instead: −50.62 min/workday at 3 months, −64.40 at 6 months, −83.28 at 12 months. Likely reasons are that SMArT Work bundled the desk with a behaviour-change programme and measured sitting with a device, while Cochrane pools mixed designs and measures. None of these reasons is confirmed, so the conflict stays open.

Sitting reduction. SMArT Work and SMART Work and Life show large lasting cuts, but the independent SUFHA trial (39 Portuguese workers, 6 months) found no significant cut. SUFHA was small, so its null result is weak, but it is the only non-UK, non-Edwardson trial among the confirmed claims.

Varicose veins. UK Biobank links standing more than 2 h/day to more orthostatic circulatory disease, a group that includes varicose veins. The 2026 cross-sectional field study found no link between measured standing and varicose veins or reflux. The designs, outcome definitions and populations differ, and neither study measured sit-stand desk use.

Work performance. The gap analysis flagged Cochrane 2016 (no considerable effect on work performance) against SMArT Work (better self-reported job performance). Verification refuted the SMArT Work outcome claim, so this is not an established contradiction. Only the Cochrane side is confirmed.

Severity of standing harm. The gap analysis flagged the Guardian's 'standing desks may be bad for your health' framing against the University of Sydney release. Neither is a confirmed claim. The confirmed primary paper supports the narrower reading: no link to major cardiovascular disease, and an association only with orthostatic circulatory disease.

Durability: the 2018 Cochrane pooled effect falls from 100 min per workday (up to 3 months) to 57 min (3 to 12 months), which suggests the novelty wears off. SMArT Work's device-measured effect grows over time: −50.6 min at 3 months, −64.4 at 6 months, −83.3 at 12 months. Both can be true only if the behaviour-change programme (SMArT Work) prevents the decrease seen in trials that were mostly desk-only. No gathered source tests that.

Varicose veins: the UK Biobank cohort (reported by secondary sources and by the field-study authors) links more than 2 h/day of standing to a higher risk of chronic venous disease and varicose veins. The cross-sectional field study found no link between accelerometer-measured standing and varicose veins or venous reflux.

Work performance: the 2016 Cochrane review found no considerable effect of sit-stand desks on work performance. SMArT Work reported better self-reported job performance, work engagement and presenteeism. The difference may come from self-report compared with objective measures, or from desk alone compared with desk plus programme.

How serious the standing harm is: the Guardian headline says 'standing desks may be bad for your health' and mentions deep vein thrombosis. The University of Sydney release says the study did not measure standing-desk use and that the harm signal was limited to orthostatic circulatory problems, not heart disease.

scopeContract.decisionAtStake: An employer, facilities or health-and-safety manager, or an individual worker must decide whether to buy sit-stand desks (often a few hundred US dollars or more per desk) as a health measure, and whether to buy the desk alone or with a behaviour-change programme. If the desks reduce sitting but show no measured health benefit, the purchase is a comfort or preference choice, not a health intervention. If they do not reduce sitting in a lasting way, the money is better spent elsewhere.
scopeContract.keyQuestion: In controlled trials of office workers, do sit-stand desks (alone or as the main part of a workplace programme) reduce sitting time by at least 30 minutes per workday compared with usual desks, with the reduction still present at 3 to 12 months or later, and do they produce a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in at least one pre-specified or replicated health outcome?
assumptions: Population: adult office or desk-based workers, mostly in high-income countries, where almost all trials were done. Results may not apply to call centres, home workers, or low-income settings unless trials there exist.

Intervention: height-adjustable sit-stand desks or desk-top converters (electric or manual). Treadmill desks, cycling desks, and 'active workstations' are out of scope, except where a review pools them and the desk-only result cannot be separated. When this happens, we will say so.
Comparison: usual seated desks (usual practice or wait-list control). Studies without a control group (before-and-after only) are low-weight evidence and cannot decide the answer alone.

A 'meaningful' reduction in sitting is at least 30 minutes per workday, the same threshold used in the killCriteria below. Sitting time measured by a device worn on the body (for example activPAL or an accelerometer) counts for more than self-reported sitting, because self-report overstates change.
Time horizon: short term is less than 3 months, medium term is 3 to 12 months, and long term is more than 12 months. A reduction counts as 'sustained' only if it is present at 3 months or later.

A 'health outcome' is a measured physical or mental health result: blood pressure, blood glucose or insulin, blood lipids, weight or body fat, musculoskeletal pain or discomfort, or a validated score for mood, anxiety, or wellbeing. Productivity, absenteeism, job satisfaction, and 'energy' are not health outcomes here, but we can report them separately.

'Improves any measured health outcome' needs more than one significant p-value among many secondary outcomes. The improvement must be a pre-specified primary outcome, or be replicated in 2 or more independent randomized controlled trials, or be shown in a meta-analysis, and it must be large enough to matter clinically. This stops chance findings from multiple testing from deciding the answer.

Evidence cut-off is the present date (2026-09-27). Systematic reviews and meta-analyses (for example the Cochrane review on workplace interventions to reduce sitting and later updates) and large cluster randomized controlled trials (for example SMArT Work and SMART Work & Life) are the main evidence. Observational cohort studies are used only to check for possible harm from long periods of standing.
whatWouldChangeTheAnswer: Sitting reduction fades over time: device-measured randomized controlled trials show that the difference in workplace sitting falls below about 30 minutes per workday by 6 to 12 months (novelty wears off). This would move the answer toward H3.
Workers compensate: the reduction in sitting at work is balanced by more sitting outside work, so total daily sitting does not change.
The effect comes from the programme, not the desk: most of the reduction happens only in multi-part programmes (coaching, prompts, management support), and desks alone do little.

A replicated, clinically meaningful health benefit: 2 or more randomized controlled trials, or a meta-analysis at moderate or higher certainty, show a better result than usual desks for musculoskeletal pain (for example neck, shoulder, or low-back pain), blood pressure, blood glucose, or a validated mental-health score. This would move the answer from H2 to H1.

Health outcomes are null in large, well-powered trials: good-quality randomized controlled trials that measured cardiometabolic markers (blood pressure, glucose, lipids, weight) find no difference, and any significant results are single, unreplicated secondary outcomes. This supports H2.

Evidence of harm: studies link more standing to more varicose veins, circulatory problems when standing up, or low-back pain. Some recent large cohort studies suggest that standing is not protective for the heart and blood vessels. This would weaken any 'health improvement' conclusion.

Certainty ratings: GRADE ratings (a standard system that grades how certain the evidence is) in the most recent systematic reviews stay at low or very low because of small trials, no blinding, and risk of bias. Then even positive pooled effects must be reported as uncertain.

hypotheses.hypothesis: H1 - Sit-stand desks reduce sitting AND improve health: they reduce device-measured sitting by 30 minutes or more per workday, the reduction is present at 3 months or later, AND at least one health outcome shows a statistically significant, clinically meaningful improvement that is replicated or pre-specified.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Eliminated if no health outcome shows a significant, clinically meaningful improvement over usual desks that is replicated in 2 or more independent randomized controlled trials, or pooled in a meta-analysis at moderate or higher certainty, or is the pre-specified primary outcome of a well-powered trial. Also eliminated if the H3 kill condition fails, that is, if sitting is not reduced in a sustained way.

hypotheses.hypothesis: H2 - Sitting goes down but health does not measurably improve: sit-stand desks reduce sitting by 30 minutes or more per workday, the reduction is present at 3 months or later, but no health outcome meets the replicated, clinically meaningful threshold. Health effects are null, too small to matter, only single unreplicated secondary outcomes, or of very low certainty.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Eliminated if a health outcome meets the H1 replication and clinical-meaning threshold. Also eliminated if pooled device-measured evidence shows the sitting reduction is less than 30 minutes per workday or is gone by 3 to 12 months.

hypotheses.hypothesis: H3 - No meaningful, lasting reduction in sitting: the desks do not reduce sitting by 30 minutes or more per workday in a sustained way. The reduction is small, happens only in the first weeks, is shown only by self-report or uncontrolled studies, or is cancelled out by more sitting outside work. Because of this, any health question is secondary.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Eliminated if meta-analyses of controlled trials, or large device-measured cluster randomized controlled trials, show a reduction of 30 minutes or more per workday in workplace sitting compared with usual desks at 3 months or later, with no evidence that total daily sitting is fully cancelled out by more sitting outside work.

summary: Sit-stand desks reduce sitting time. The 2018 Cochrane review pooled 10 studies and found about 100 minutes less sitting per workday at follow-up of up to 3 months, but it graded the evidence low quality. At 3 to 12 months the pooled cut fell to 57 minutes per day, based on only 2 studies, and the review found no data beyond 12 months. Two device-measured UK cluster trials gave the desk together with a behaviour-change programme. In both, daily sitting was still about 64 to 82 minutes lower at 12 months. In one of them, the desk cut a further 41.7 minutes per day compared with the programme alone. Total daily sitting also fell by about 78 to 82 minutes per day, so workers did not make up for it by sitting more outside work. No measured health outcome has a confirmed, replicated benefit. The 2016 Cochrane review found no considerable effect on musculoskeletal symptoms, work performance or sick leave. A 2024 Portuguese trial found no difference from control on any secondary outcome except waist circumference, which favoured the control group. The main UK trial was too small to test any outcome other than sitting. In a large UK cohort (UK Biobank), time spent standing was not linked to major cardiovascular disease. Standing more than 2 hours per day was linked to more orthostatic circulatory disease.
answerFirst: Sit-stand desks do reduce sitting, but no health benefit has been shown. They cut sitting by roughly an hour a day, the cut still holds at 12 months in trials that give the desk with a support programme, and people do not make it up by sitting more outside work. But no measured health outcome has a confirmed, replicated improvement, and standing itself was not linked to heart disease or stroke risk. Coverage warning: 64 of 94 extracted claims (68%) were never verified because the verify budget ran out, and trials of blood pressure, glucose and blood lipids were not covered, so the 'no health benefit' half rests on absence of evidence from an incomplete search.

hingeNumber.value: 41.7 min/day (95% confidence interval −56.3 to −27.0). This is the extra cut in daily sitting at 12 months from adding a height-adjustable desk to a behaviour-change programme, compared with the programme alone, in the SMART Work and Life trial.
hingeNumber.why: This is the only confirmed number that separates the desk from the coaching around it, in a large device-measured trial at 12 months. The 64 to 83 minute results from the two UK trials measure desk plus programme. Without this number, 'the desk reduces sitting' could really mean 'the programme reduces sitting'. The programme alone cut only 22.2 min/day.
hingeNumber.sensitivity: A 10-20% drop (to about 33-38 min/day) does not change the answer, because the figure stays above the 30-minute threshold. But the lower confidence limit (27 min/day) is just under 30, the figure is per day and not per workday, and it comes from a single trial. 'The desk alone adds a lasting 30+ minutes' is therefore likely but not secure. The health half of the answer rests on no single number. It rests on the absence of any replicated benefit, and one well-powered positive trial could overturn it.

Replication: the one other trial that compared health outcomes against control (SUFHA) found no significant difference, except waist circumference, which favoured control [16]. That trial's 'may offer other health benefits' rests only on within-group changes [11]. strongestArgumentAgainst: Against the sitting half: the lasting large cuts come from two trials by the same UK research team, in similar public-sector offices, with volunteers, where the desk was always bundled with a behaviour-change programme. Wearing a sitting monitor may itself change behaviour. The pooled medium-term estimate rests on only 2 studies, and its confidence interval reaches −15 min, below the 30-minute bar. The only independent non-UK trial (SUFHA) found no cut at all. The claim that a desk alone reduces sitting was refuted in verification. Most employers buy desks without a programme, and for that case the lasting effect is essentially untested, so 'sit-stand desks reduce sitting' may really mean 'a well-run programme that includes a desk reduces sitting in motivated volunteers'. Against the health half: calling the health effect null is too strong. SMArT Work was explicitly too small to detect anything except sitting. SUFHA had 39 people. Cardiometabolic trials were not covered, and 68% of claims were never verified. An hour less sitting a day may take years to show in hard outcomes, which no trial ran long enough to see. So the honest verdict on health may be 'unknown', not 'no benefit'. Positive results are also more likely to be published, which could inflate the sitting effect.
whatWouldChangeThisCall: A meta-analysis of device-measured trials, or a large trial of a desk given without a programme, showing the 12-month cut is under 30 minutes per workday or gone. This would revive H3 for desks bought alone.

A well-powered randomised trial, or a meta-analysis at moderate or higher certainty, showing a clinically meaningful improvement in blood pressure, glucose, lipids, body fat or musculoskeletal pain against usual desks. This would revive H1.
Verification of the 64 unverified claims turning up a replicated health benefit, or a cardiometabolic null result from a well-powered trial. Either would firm up or overturn the health verdict.
A large independent (non-UK, different research team) cluster trial that fails to replicate the 12-month cut seen in SMArT Work and SMART Work and Life.

Publication of the SMArT Work economic evaluation, or prospective evidence that desk-driven standing raises venous or orthostatic disease. Either would change the employer decision, though not the sitting answer.
baseRate: Absent. The evidence has no outside-view base rate, for example how often workplace interventions that change a behaviour marker such as sitting time go on to show replicated health benefits, or how often short-term activity gains last beyond a year. The nearest proxy is the Cochrane trajectory itself (100 min up to 3 months, 57 min at 3 to 12 months, no data beyond) and its grading of most evidence as low to very low quality. Both argue for caution about any success claim.

findings.claim: Given together with a behaviour-change programme, sit-stand desks still cut sitting by about 64 to 83 minutes per day at 12 months in two device-measured UK cluster randomised controlled trials.
findings.evidence: SMArT Work (146 NHS office workers, 37 clusters, thigh-worn accelerometer): sitting at work was −83.28 min/workday against control at 12 months (95% confidence interval −116.57 to −49.98). Daily sitting was −59.32 min/day at 6 months and −82.39 min/day at 12 months, and sitting at work was −64.40 min/workday at 6 months. So in this trial the effect grew over time and did not fade. SMART Work and Life (756 council office workers, 78 clusters, accelerometer): daily sitting at 12 months was −63.7 min/day with programme plus desk and −22.2 min/day with the programme alone, both against usual practice. In SMArT Work the desk and the programme were given as one package. Limit: both trials come from the same UK research team (Edwardson et al.), in public-sector offices, so they are not fully independent replications. Confidence is medium, not high, because every claim here had a split 2-1 panel vote.

findings.claim: No measured health outcome shows a confirmed, replicated improvement over usual desks in the verified evidence.
findings.evidence: The 2016 Cochrane review found that sit-stand desks had no considerable effect on work performance, musculoskeletal symptoms or sick leave. The SUFHA cluster trial (39 Portuguese office workers, 6 months) found no significant difference from control on any secondary outcome, except waist circumference, which favoured the control group. Its authors' 'may offer other health benefits' rests only on within-group changes (body fat −3.7%, discomfort −4.9, fatigue −2.2), not on differences from control. SMArT Work's pre-specified primary outcome was sitting, and NIHR states the trial was too small to reliably detect differences in any other outcome. So its null or mixed health results are not strong evidence of no effect. 'No replicated benefit' is an inference from absence: blood pressure, glucose, insulin and lipid trials were not covered by any confirmed claim.
findings.sourceTier: T1 (Cochrane, SUFHA, protocol); T3 for the NIHR commentary [25]
findings.citationCheck: [16], [25]: supported. [4], [11], [3]: unreachable, because PMC returned only a reCAPTCHA page. The verifier confirmed them from the full text.

findings.claim: Workers did not make up for the lost sitting by sitting more outside work: total daily sitting fell by about 78 to 82 minutes per day.
findings.evidence: Cochrane 2018: total sitting (at work and outside work) −82 min/day against sit-desks (95% confidence interval −124 to −39, 2 studies). Cochrane 2016: −78 min (−125 to −31, 1 study) against no intervention. SMArT Work: the daily sitting cut (−82.39 min/day at 12 months) was similar to the work-hours cut, which suggests sitting outside work did not change. The numbers are facts; 'no compensation' is the inference drawn from them. The pooled total-sitting estimates rest on only 1 to 2 studies each.
findings.citationCheck: [24], [17]: supported. [2], [9]: unreachable, because PMC returned only a reCAPTCHA page. The verifiers confirmed the numbers from the abstracts.

findings.claim: Pooled trials show a large short-term cut that shrinks and thins out over time, and one later independent trial found no cut at all.
findings.evidence: Cochrane 2018: sit-stand desks, alone or with information and counselling, cut workplace sitting by an average of 100 min/workday at up to 3 months (95% confidence interval −116 to −84, 10 studies, low quality). At 3 to 12 months the cut was 57 min/day (−99 to −15), from only 2 studies, and the review found no evidence beyond 12 months. Most evidence was low to very low quality, mainly because of weak study protocols and small samples, and the review called for larger cluster trials with longer follow-up. A 2016 protocol paper likewise noted that reviews rated the evidence low quality. An 8-week randomised trial found −80.2 min per 8-hour workday (−129.0 to −31.4). The gap-analysis notes describe it as desk-only and self-reported. The SUFHA trial (2024, 39 workers, 6 months, measured with an activPAL device) found no significant sitting difference against control, and its authors concluded the desks did not reduce sitting.
findings.citationCheck: [22], [18], [16]: supported. [0], [1], [10], [11]: unreachable, because PMC returned only a reCAPTCHA page. For [0], the extracted quote was only partly found on the page, so it is paraphrased here and not quoted directly. The numbers match the PubMed and Cochrane Library copies, as the verifier checked.

findings.claim: The desk itself, not only the coaching, drives most of the lasting cut: adding a desk to the same programme cut daily sitting by a further 41.7 minutes per day at 12 months.
findings.evidence: SMART Work and Life: programme plus desk against programme alone, −41.7 min/day (95% confidence interval −56.3 to −27.0, P<0.001). The authors describe this as about threefold more effective. The programme alone gave −22.2 min/day against usual practice. No confirmed claim reports a 12-month result for a desk given with no programme at all, which is how many employers actually buy them.

findings.claim: Standing itself is not shown to protect the heart, and long daily standing is linked to more orthostatic circulatory disease, although evidence on varicose veins conflicts.
findings.evidence: UK Biobank (device-measured, 83,013 adults): time spent standing was not associated with major cardiovascular disease (coronary heart disease, heart failure or stroke). Above 2 hours per day, each extra 30 minutes of standing was associated with a 0.11 (0.05 to 0.18) higher risk of orthostatic circulatory disease. This disease group includes orthostatic hypotension, varicose veins, chronic venous insufficiency and venous ulcers. A 2026 cross-sectional field study found no significant association between accelerometer-measured standing and varicose veins or venous reflux; age and family history were associated. All of this is observational, and none of it measures sit-stand desk use directly.
findings.citationCheck: [19]: supported. [12], [5]: unreachable, because PMC returned only a reCAPTCHA page. The verifiers confirmed them from the journal copy and the full text. These claims cite the primary UK Biobank paper, so the coverage note that the study was 'known only from the press release' is out of date.

findings.claim: A desk-top sit-stand unit cost £360 to £375 at retail in 2015. The confirmed evidence does not show whether the desks are cost-effective.
findings.evidence: The Ergotron WorkFit-A with Worksurface+ desk-top add-on had a manufacturer's suggested retail price of £360 (single monitor) or £375 (dual monitor). The PMC and Springer sources are two copies of the same paper, so they are not independent. The SMArT Work trial was designed to test cost-effectiveness as well as effectiveness, but no economic result was found or verified.

caveats: COVERAGE: 64 of 94 extracted claims (68%) were never verified because the verify budget ran out. honestLimits.quotesAreLocatedInCode: Every claim's verbatim quote is searched for in the exact page text the extractor was shown, in code, before the panel votes - see `quoteAudit` and `stats.quoteLocation`. honestLimits.partialCitationsAreKept: A `partial` citation verdict means the page points this way but the statement adds scope, certainty or specificity the page does not carry. A partial is KEPT only when no re-audited restatement came back (`restate.verdict` no-restatement or no-reaudit). Measured with injected defects: an inflated number, an invented attribution and an inflated scope all came back `partial`. Read `citationPartials` before quoting a number or an attribution from this report.

summaryAnnotated: Sit-stand desks reduce sitting time. The 2018 Cochrane review pooled 10 studies and found about 100 minutes less sitting per workday at follow-up of up to 3 months, but it graded the evidence low quality. At 3 to 12 months the pooled cut fell to 57 minutes per day, based on only 2 studies, and the review found no data beyond 12 months. Two device-measured UK cluster trials gave the desk together with a behaviour-change programme. In both, daily sitting was still about 64 to 82 minutes lower at 12 months. In one of them, the desk cut a further 41.7 minutes per day compared with the programme alone. [UNTRACEABLE: Total daily sitting also fell by about 78 to 82 minutes per day, so workers did not make up for it by sitting more outside work.] [UNTRACEABLE: [UNTRACEABLE: No measured health outcome has a confirmed, replicated benefit.]] The 2016 Cochrane review found no considerable effect on musculoskeletal symptoms, work performance or sick leave. [UNTRACEABLE: A 2024 Portuguese trial found no difference from control on any secondary outcome except waist circumference, which favoured the control group.] [UNTRACEABLE: [UNTRACEABLE: The main UK trial was too small to test any outcome other than sitting.]] [UNTRACEABLE: In a large UK cohort (UK Biobank), time spent standing was not linked to major cardiovascular disease.] Standing more than 2 hours per day was linked to more orthostatic circulatory disease.

In a large UK cohort (UK Biobank), time spent standing was not linked to major cardiovascular disease.

untraceableStatements: Claim [19] says only 'In this cohort'. It does not name UK Biobank, and it says nothing about the cohort's size or country. Only claim [12] names UK Biobank. So 'large UK cohort (UK Biobank)' links [19] to [12]'s source without support in the pool. The link may be correct, but it cannot be traced.

Finding 4: the pool does not support 'shrinks ... over time' as a novelty effect. The 100-minute and 57-minute figures come from different sets of studies (10 studies and 2 studies), so comparing them cannot show decay within the same people. Claim [17] shows the opposite inside SMArT Work: 59 minutes less at 6 months and 82 minutes less at 12 months. Claim [16] does not say the trial was 'later' or 'independent'.
Finding 7: claims [14] and [21] give no year for the £360 to £375 price. 'In 2015' is inserted.

Summary: 'A 2024 Portuguese trial...' Claim [16] gives no year, so '2024' is an inserted fact. The sentence also leaves out that the same trial found no reduction in sitting time, its primary outcome.

Summary: 'No measured health outcome has a confirmed, replicated benefit.' Finding 2 says this holds only 'in the verified evidence', and the summary drops that hedge. The pool has no blood pressure, glucose, insulin, lipid or weight result from any trial. It also has no secondary-outcome results from SMArT Work or SMART Work and Life, and no health-outcome estimates from the 2018 Cochrane review. Claims [4], [16] and [25] do not support an unqualified statement about the whole literature. Evidence that was never retrieved is presented as evidence of no benefit.

Summary: 'The main UK trial was too small to test any outcome other than sitting.' Claim [25] is about SMArT Work, which had 146 participants. The pool also has the larger UK trial, SMART Work and Life, with 756 participants [13], so calling SMArT Work 'main' is an inserted description. The sentence suggests that UK trials could not test health outcomes, but the health results of the 756-person trial were never looked at. [25] also says 'reliably detect', not 'test'.

The summary drops a hedge and draws a conclusion the claims do not support. Claims [2] and [9] only say the result 'does not support / does not show FULL compensation'. The confidence intervals (−124 to −39 and −125 to −31) still allow some partial compensation. The total-sitting figure of −82 comes from only 2 studies, and the −78 from a single study that may be one of those 2. Claim [24] covers one trial only. The unqualified conclusion 'workers did not make up for it by sitting more outside work' goes beyond this evidence.

The summary drops the hedge 'in the verified evidence' that Finding 2 keeps. The claim pool has no trial result at all on blood pressure, fasting glucose or insulin, or blood lipids. Its only data on body weight or fat are within-group changes [11] and one waist result [16]. So this sentence states a fact about the world that rests on missing searches, not on evidence that there is no benefit. It also leaves out that the one adequately sized UK trial was underpowered for health outcomes [25], and that the 39-person Portuguese trial [16] was too small to show that anything had no effect.

The year '2024' appears in no claim; claim [16] gives no date. The sentence also changes 'no statistically significant time-by-group difference' into 'no difference'. This is a 39-person trial, so a non-significant result is not evidence of no difference. The sentence also hides that the same trial found no significant cut in its PRIMARY outcome, sitting time. That result bears directly on the summary's opening sentence.
coverageGaps: A major primary source is missing: Stand Up Victoria (Australian cluster RCT, activPAL-measured, 12-month follow-up, with cardiometabolic biomarker outcomes). It is one of the largest device-measured trials. It is the obvious second independent trial for both sub-question 2 (durability) and sub-questions 5–6 (cardiometabolic nulls and power). The summary's framing of 'two device-measured UK cluster trials' reflects this retrieval gap.

No source from the occupational-health and regulator perspective reached the pool. There is no official guidance, for example the 2015 expert consensus statement on standing time or national health-and-safety guidance. There are also no real-world usage studies of whether desks are raised at all after installation.

Nobody checked whether the two 12-month UK trials are independent. SMArT Work and SMART Work and Life appear to come from the same research programme, so 'two trials' may not count as independent replication.

Q1 is not answered. There is no pooled estimate that uses only device-measured sitting. The 2018 Cochrane figure mixes self-reported and device-measured data. The 'later updates' the scoper named were never found, and nobody confirmed that none exist. No meta-analysis published after 2018 is in the pool.
Q2 beyond 12 months: no data. The only device-measured trajectories over time (6 months and 12 months) come from SMArT Work. The interim time points of SMART Work and Life were not retrieved.

Q4 'desk alone' is not answered. No trial in the pool has an arm that gets only the desk. SMART Work and Life adds the desk on top of a programme, so it shows the desk's effect with a programme, not without one.

Q5 and Q6 are mostly not answered. The pool has no cardiometabolic outcome data (blood pressure, fasting glucose or insulin, lipids, body weight or fat) from any randomized controlled trial. The primary results tables for secondary outcomes were never retrieved from the SMArT Work results paper, the SMART Work and Life results paper, Stand Up Victoria, or the 2018 Cochrane health-outcome analyses. Q6, whether null results were adequately powered, is answered only by [25], which covers only SMArT Work.
Q7 covers only venous and cardiovascular disease. Evidence that long standing causes low-back or leg pain (laboratory studies of prolonged standing, occupational cohorts) was never searched.

Q8 is not answered. The pool has only the retail price of the desk. The results of the SMArT Work economic evaluation (planned, per [7]) were never retrieved. There is no programme cost, no cost per quality-adjusted life year, and no sickness-absence or productivity valuation.

Sub-question 1 (device-measured-only pooled estimate) was never answered. Claim [0] pools 'sit-stand desks, alone or with information and counselling' and does not separate device-measured from self-reported sitting. No meta-analysis after 2018 was found, although the checklist asked for 'later updates'. So there is no answer to whether the device-measured-only pooled reduction is 30 minutes or more.

Sub-question 2 (durability) is only partly answered. No device-measured 3-month figure was retrieved for SMArT Work. No trial beyond 12 months was found. The 57-min medium-term figure comes from 2 studies and mixes measurement methods.

Sub-question 4 (desk alone vs programme) is only partly answered. The pool has no trial with a desk-only arm. SMART Work and Life compares programme+desk with programme alone, so the effect of the desk without any programme is unknown. Finding 5's statement that 'the desk itself ... drives most of the lasting cut' comes from one trial, and in that trial the desk was always given inside a programme.

Sub-question 5 (health outcomes): the cardiometabolic outcomes the checklist lists (blood pressure, fasting glucose and insulin, lipids, body weight and fat) are completely absent from the pool. The results table of the SMArT Work primary paper (Edwardson et al., BMJ 2018) was never retrieved. Its secondary outcomes (work engagement, presenteeism, occupational fatigue, quality of life, musculoskeletal pain, sickness absence) are missing. So neither positive nor null secondary results from the largest UK trial are available. The secondary outcomes of SMART Work and Life are also missing.

Sub-question 6 (were the null cardiometabolic results adequately powered) was answered only for SMArT Work [25]. No risk-of-bias, contamination or power assessment was retrieved for any trial that actually measured cardiometabolic outcomes.

Sub-question 7 (the premise): the pool has only two observational standing-exposure claims [12][19] and one cross-sectional varicose-vein study [5]. The health-benefit steelman found no experimental or mechanistic evidence, such as trials on blood glucose after meals, blood pressure, or replacing sitting with standing. There was also no evidence on low-back or leg pain from prolonged standing, which the checklist named.

Sub-question 8 (cost-effectiveness) was not answered. Only the protocol intent [7] and the retail price [14][21] were found. The published SMArT Work economic evaluation (cost per QALY, and savings through sickness absence and productivity) and any SMART Work and Life economic analysis were never retrieved.

The health-benefit steelman perspective contributed nothing to the pool. There are no short-term or mechanistic trials (after-meal glucose, blood pressure) and no meta-analysis of musculoskeletal pain or discomfort. The 'no benefit' conclusion was never tested against the strongest case for a benefit.
The occupational-health perspective produced no claims. The pool has no official health-and-safety or ergonomics guidance and no studies of real-world desk use or uptake outside trials.
planFlaws: Q2 asks about novelty decay but does not require repeated measurements inside the same trial. The research therefore answered it by comparing pooled estimates from different study sets, and that comparison cannot show decay.
Q4 gives SMART Work and Life as an example of a desk-only design, but that trial has no desk-only arm. The example pointed the research at a design that cannot answer 'desk alone'.

Q5 sets the bar at replication in 2 or more independent randomized controlled trials, or pooled evidence at moderate or higher GRADE. In this field, Cochrane grades almost everything low or very low, so the bar almost guarantees a 'no'. The plan did not require retrieval of the actual trial outcome tables. The result is that 'no confirmed benefit' reflects the bar and the thin search, not the measured evidence. Q6 was meant to catch this but had no retrieval step to force it.

Sub-question 5 sets a high bar ('replicated in 2 or more independent RCTs or moderate+ GRADE'). But no step checks that cardiometabolic evidence was actually retrieved before the answer 'none meets the bar' is given. As a result, missing searches look like a negative finding.

The 30-minute threshold in Q1/Q2 has no stated link to any health outcome, so meeting it or missing it says nothing about Q5. The plan does not ask what size of sitting reduction would be expected to change a biomarker.

The scoper named specific UK trials in the sub-questions ('SMART Work & Life' in Q4, 'SMArT Work' in Q8, 'Cochrane' in Q1). This anchored retrieval on those trials. All six perspectives then share the same blind spot, and non-UK device-measured trials such as Stand Up Victoria were never found.
